- If sentiment is positive (≥0.2) in recent history, model tends to underreact — increase forecast slightly to align with bullish momentum.  
- If model shows gradual upward drift (e.g., +0.1–0.3 per day) but true outcome spikes sharply, reduce forecast slope to avoid overshoot.  
- When true outcome exceeds model by >5% over 3–5 days, consider mean reversion bias — adjust forecast downward slightly to reflect diminishing momentum.  
- If model forecast is flat or slightly declining while true outcome is rising, add a small upward bias (e.g., +0.5–1.0) to capture lagged momentum.  
- In high-sentiment periods (e.g., 0.3+), model often underestimates peak — apply a “sentiment multiplier” to forecast, e.g., +10–20% for sentiment >0.2.  
- If model forecast is consistently below true outcome by 2–3% over 10+ days, consider “baseline drift” — add a small upward offset to forecast to account for persistent upward bias.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows strong upward trend after a dip, model often overcorrects — reduce forecast slope to avoid overestimating continuation.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0) and model forecast is rising, consider “bearish correction” — reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0 to reflect pessimism.  
- When true outcome is volatile and model is smooth, apply “volatility smoothing” — adjust forecast to match recent true outcome variance.  
- If model forecast is above true outcome by >10% for 3+ consecutive days, consider “overfitting correction” — reduce forecast by 1–2% per day to avoid overestimation.
